learn: Why the race-car MDP is a useful shared benchmark
Monte Carlo returns and first- vs every-visit estimates from one episode
TD(0) prediction, SARSA, Expected SARSA and Q-learning on the same transitions
DP vs Monte Carlo vs TD: model, bootstrapping, timing and variance
intro.why: Seeing every method applied to the same tiny problem, with the same episode, makes their differences concrete: what target each one uses, when it can update, and what it converges to.

symbols: the two tables in Double Q-learning

sections.title: The race car as a shared benchmark
sections.plain: Take the solved race car, hide the model, and learn from driving.
sections.body:
The race-car MDP of M4 (Cool/Warm/Overheated; Slow/Fast) has a known answer: $v_* = (15.5, 14.5, 0)$, $q_*(C,\text{slow}) = 14.95$, $q_*(C,\text{fast}) = 15.5$, $q_*(W,\text{slow}) = 14.5$, $q_*(W,\text{fast}) = -10$, policy Cool → Fast, Warm → Slow. DP got this using the model. Now we pretend the model is unknown and learn from experience, using one recorded episode throughout:

$$C \xrightarrow{F,\,+2} W \xrightarrow{S,\,+1} C \xrightarrow{F,\,+2} W \xrightarrow{F,\,-10} O$$

Every method below is GPI; they differ only in how they evaluate: sampled full returns (Monte Carlo) or bootstrapped one-step targets (TD).

sections.title: Monte Carlo returns from one episode
sections.plain: Wait for the episode to end, compute the actual returns, average them.
sections.body:
With $\gamma = 0.6$ and rewards $R_1..R_4 = 2, 1, 2, -10$, compute returns backwards with $G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}$:

$$G_3 = -10,\quad G_2 = 2 + 0.6(-10) = -4,\quad G_1 = 1 + 0.6(-4) = -1.4,\quad G_0 = 2 + 0.6(-1.4) = 1.16$$

First-visit MC uses the return after the first occurrence of each state–action pair in the episode: $Q(C,F) \leftarrow 1.16$, $Q(W,S) \leftarrow -1.4$, $Q(W,F) \leftarrow -10$. The second visit of $(C,F)$ ($G_2 = -4$) is ignored. Every-visit MC averages all occurrences: $Q(C,F) = (1.16-4)/2 = -1.42$.

MC needs no model and no bootstrapping, but it must wait for the episode to end, and its estimates have high variance (one episode's luck dominates). After improvement the policy shifts away from Fast-when-Warm, which ended this episode badly.

sections.title: Off-policy weighting of an episode
sections.plain: Learn about one policy while following another, reweighting by how likely each action was under each.
sections.body:
Off-policy MC learns about a target policy $\pi$ (e.g. greedy) from episodes generated by a behaviour policy $b$ (e.g. exploratory or logged). Returns are reweighted by

$$W = \prod_{k=t}^{T-1}\frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{b(A_k\mid S_k)}$$

Worked weight. Deterministic target ($\pi(\text{Slow}\mid\text{Warm}) = 1$), behaviour $b(\text{Slow}\mid\text{Warm}) = 0.4$: a matching step has $W = 1/0.4 = 2.5$. A step where the behaviour takes an action the target never would ($\pi = 0$) makes $W = 0$: that step and everything earlier in the episode contribute nothing, so off-policy MC learns only from episode tails where the two policies agree.

Two estimators: ordinary importance sampling (unbiased, high variance) and weighted importance sampling (normalised by the sum of weights: biased, much lower variance, usually preferred). M7 covers both in depth.

sections.title: TD(0) prediction
sections.plain: Update a state's value after every step toward the reward plus the next state's estimate.
sections.body:
$$V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\big[\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})}_{\text{TD target}} - V(S_t)\big]$$

TD combines MC's model-free sampling with DP's bootstrapping. Worked ($\gamma = 0.9$, $\alpha = 0.5$, $V = 0$): transition $C \to W$ with reward 2: target $2 + 0.9\cdot0 = 2$, TD error 2, $V(C) = 0 + 0.5\cdot2 = 1$. Next $W \to C$ with reward 1: $V(W) = 0 + 0.5[1 + 0.9\cdot1 - 0] = 0.95$. Learning happened during the episode, with no waiting for the end, and the second update already used the first.

This is exactly the tic-tac-toe rule from M1, now with rewards and discounting.

sections.title: SARSA
sections.plain: On-policy TD control: update Q toward reward plus the value of the action you actually take next.
sections.body:
SARSA is named after the quintuple it uses, $(S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})$:

$$Q(S_t,A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma Q(S_{t+1},A_{t+1}) - Q(S_t,A_t)\big]$$

Worked ($\gamma = 0.9$, $\alpha = 0.8$, all $Q = 0$): $(C,F,2,W,S)$: $Q(C,F) = 0.8[2 + 0.9\cdot0] = 1.6$. $(W,S,1,C,F)$: $Q(W,S) = 0.8[1 + 0.9\cdot1.6] = 1.952$. Later $(W,F,-10,O)$: $Q(W,F) = 0.8[-10] = -8$: SARSA has felt the danger of Fast when Warm.

SARSA evaluates the policy it actually follows, exploration included, so with ε-greedy behaviour it learns the values of the ε-greedy policy, not $q_*$. In ex2 those values are about 11 for Cool, well below 15.5, because random Fast-when-Warm moves sometimes overheat the engine.

sections.title: Expected SARSA and Q-learning
sections.plain: Average over next actions (Expected SARSA) or take the best one (Q-learning).
sections.body:
Expected SARSA replaces the sampled next action by its expectation under the policy, lowering variance:

$$Q(S_t,A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\Big[R_{t+1} + \gamma\sum_a\pi(a\mid S_{t+1})Q(S_{t+1},a) - Q(S_t,A_t)\Big]$$

With equiprobable next actions and all $Q = 0$: expected next value $0.5\cdot0 + 0.5\cdot0 = 0$, so $Q(C,F) = 0.8[2] = 1.6$, the same as SARSA at first; the benefit (less noise) appears later.

Q-learning bootstraps from the best next action regardless of what the behaviour does: it is off-policy and learns $q_*$ directly.

$$Q(S_t,A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma\max_{a'}Q(S_{t+1},a') - Q(S_t,A_t)\big]$$

Worked: $Q(C,F) = 0.8[2 + 0.9\max(0,0)] = 1.6$. Suppose a later transition $(W,S,+20,C)$ with $Q(C,F) = 1.6$: $Q(W,S) = 0.8[20 + 0.9\cdot1.6] = 17.15$: the max pulls value from the best next action, not the one taken. Expected SARSA with a greedy target policy is Q-learning.

Code example ex2 (5,000 ε-greedy episodes): Q-learning ≈ (14.95, 15.41, 14.40, −10), close to $q_*$; SARSA and Expected SARSA ≈ 10–11, the value of the ε-greedy policy itself (exact: $q(C,F) = 10.98$, $q(C,S) = 10.88$). That 0.1 margin is so small that constant-α SARSA's noisy estimates can rank Slow above Fast in Cool.

sections.title: Double Q-learning
sections.plain: Use one table to choose the best next action and the other to score it, so noise doesn't inflate values.
sections.body:
The max in Q-learning causes maximisation bias: with noisy estimates, $\mathbb E[\max_a \hat Q(a)] \ge \max_a \mathbb E[\hat Q(a)]$, so values are systematically too high. Double Q-learning keeps two tables and decouples selection from evaluation:

$$Q_1(S_t,A_t) \leftarrow Q_1(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\Big[R_{t+1} + \gamma\,Q_2\big(S_{t+1}, \arg\max_{a'}Q_1(S_{t+1},a')\big) - Q_1(S_t,A_t)\Big]$$

and symmetrically with the roles swapped, choosing which table to update at random each step; act on $Q_1 + Q_2$.

Worked. Updating $Q_2(C,F)$ on $(C,F,2,W)$: $Q_2$ selects $\arg\max_a Q_2(W,a)$ = Fast (a tie broken toward Fast); $Q_1$ evaluates it, $Q_1(W,\text{Fast}) = 5$; so $Q_2(C,F) = 0.8[2 + 0.9\cdot5] = 5.2$. Because one table selects and the other evaluates, an overestimate in one table is not automatically used to inflate the update.

sections.title: DP vs Monte Carlo vs TD
sections.plain: Planner with a map, explorer who waits for the end, learner who updates every step.
sections.body:
DPMonte CarloTD
Needs model?Yes (full p)NoNo
Bootstraps?YesNoYes
Updates when?Every sweepEnd of episodeEvery step
Backup widthAll next statesOne trajectoryOne next state
VarianceNone (exact expectation)HighLower

Backup diagrams: DP backs up from all successors, one level deep (wide and shallow; needs the model). MC backs up along one full trajectory to the end (narrow and deep). TD backs up from one sampled successor, one step (narrow and shallow).

All three are GPI and differ only in evaluation: known dynamics (DP), sampled returns (MC) or bootstrapped one-step targets (TD). Deep RL replaces the tables with neural networks but keeps these exact updates.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Truncated episodes. Our race-car episodes are capped at 60 steps; TD bootstraps across the cut, but MC returns are slightly truncated (by γ⁶⁰ ≈ 0.002 here). In long tasks, truncation must be handled explicitly (bootstrap at the cut, not treat it as terminal).
  • On-policy safety. SARSA's lower values are not a bug: they correctly reflect that exploration sometimes overheats the engine; if you keep exploring in deployment, SARSA's policy is the safer one (cliff walking, M8).
  • Double DQN (M10) applies the double-estimator idea to deep networks using the online and target networks.

code.title: One episode through every update rule
code.explain: Recomputes all worked numbers: MC returns (1.16, −1.4, −4, −10) with first- and every-visit Q, the IS weight 2.5, TD(0) (1, 0.95), SARSA (1.6, 1.952, …, −8), Expected SARSA and Q-learning (1.6), Q-learning with reward 20 (17.152) and Double Q (5.2).
mistakes: Computing returns forwards and reusing the wrong suffix.
Using the greedy next action in SARSA.
code.notes: Note SARSA's third update revisits (C, F): 1.6 + 0.8(2 + 0.9·0 − 1.6) = 1.92, since Q(W, Fast) is still 0.
code.code:
"""One race-car episode, processed by every method of the session.

Episode: C, Fast, +2, W, Slow, +1, C, Fast, +2, W, Fast, -10, Overheated (terminal).
"""
ep = [("C", "F", 2, "W"), ("W", "S", 1, "C"), ("C", "F", 2, "W"), ("W", "F", -10, "O")]

# --- Monte Carlo (gamma = 0.6): returns computed backwards, first-visit assignment
g = 0.6; G = 0.0; returns = []
for s, a, r, s2 in reversed(ep):
    G = r + g * G; returns.append(G)
returns.reverse()
print("MC returns G0..G3 (gamma 0.6):", [round(x, 3) for x in returns])
first = {}
for t, (s, a, r, s2) in enumerate(ep):
    first.setdefault((s, a), returns[t])
print("first-visit Q:", {f"{k[0]},{k[1]}": round(v, 3) for k, v in first.items()})
every = {}
for t, (s, a, r, s2) in enumerate(ep):
    every.setdefault((s, a), []).append(returns[t])
print("every-visit Q:", {f"{k[0]},{k[1]}": round(sum(v) / len(v), 3) for k, v in every.items()})

# --- importance-sampling weight for one matching step: pi(Slow|Warm) = 1, b(Slow|Warm) = 0.4
print("IS weight W = 1/0.4 =", 1 / 0.4)

# --- TD(0) prediction (gamma 0.9, alpha 0.5) on the first two transitions
V = {"C": 0.0, "W": 0.0, "O": 0.0}
for s, a, r, s2 in ep[:2]:
    V[s] += 0.5 * (r + 0.9 * V[s2] - V[s])
print("TD(0) after two steps: V(C) =", V["C"], " V(W) =", round(V["W"], 4))

# --- SARSA (gamma 0.9, alpha 0.8): needs the next action actually taken
Q = {(s, a): 0.0 for s in "CW" for a in "SF"}; Q[("O", "-")] = 0.0
nxt = [ep[i + 1][1] if i + 1 < len(ep) else "-" for i in range(len(ep))]
for (s, a, r, s2), a2 in zip(ep, nxt):
    Q[(s, a)] += 0.8 * (r + 0.9 * Q[(s2, a2)] - Q[(s, a)])
    print(f"  SARSA  Q({s},{a}) <- {Q[(s, a)]:.3f}")

# --- Expected SARSA first step, next actions equiprobable; Q-learning first step
Q0 = {(s, a): 0.0 for s in "CW" for a in "SF"}
exp_next = 0.5 * Q0[("W", "S")] + 0.5 * Q0[("W", "F")]
print("Expected SARSA Q(C,F) =", 0.8 * (2 + 0.9 * exp_next))
print("Q-learning   Q(C,F) =", 0.8 * (2 + 0.9 * max(Q0[("W", "S")], Q0[("W", "F")])))
Q0[("C", "F")] = 1.6
print("Q-learning with a large reward (W,S,+20,C): Q(W,S) =", round(0.8 * (20 + 0.9 * max(Q0[("C", "S")], Q0[("C", "F")])), 3))

# --- Double Q: table Q2 selects, table Q1 evaluates
Q1 = {("W", "S"): 0.0, ("W", "F"): 5.0}; Q2 = {("W", "S"): 0.0, ("W", "F"): 0.0}
a_star = max(["F", "S"], key=lambda a: Q2[("W", a)])          # tie broken toward Fast
print("Double Q: select", a_star, "with Q2, evaluate with Q1 =", Q1[("W", a_star)], "-> Q2(C,F) =", 0.8 * (2 + 0.9 * Q1[("W", a_star)]))
